content: 1. Lifelong Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) for Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women with HIV: It is strongly recommended that all pregnant and breastfeeding women diagnosed with HIV initiate lifelong ART, particularly in settings with generalized epidemics. This recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence. In some countries, for women who are not eligible for ART for their own health, stopping the antiretroviral (ARV) regimen may be considered after the risk of mother-to-child transmission has ceased. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 2. Breastfeeding and ARV Interventions: National health authorities should decide whether to counsel and support HIV-positive mothers to either breastfeed with ARV interventions or avoid breastfeeding entirely, depending on the local context. In settings where breastfeeding is promoted, HIV-positive mothers should exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for up to 12 months. Breastfeeding should only stop when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence for the first six months and low-quality evidence for the 12-month duration. 3. Initiating ART in Children with HIV: ART should be initiated in all children under five years of age with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. Infants diagnosed within the first year of life should start ART immediately (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Children aged one to less than five years should also start ART, though this is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. For children aged five years and older, ART should be initiated if their CD4 count is ≤500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage. A CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³ warrants a strong recommendation, while a count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³ is a conditional recommendation. ART should also be initiated in children with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4), regardless of age or CD4 count. Any child under 18 months with a presumptive clinical diagnosis of HIV should start ART immediately (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). 4. First-Line ART Regimens for Adults and Pregnant Women: The preferred first-line ART regimen for adults, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, is a fixed-dose combination of Tenofovir (TDF), Lamivudine (3TC) or Emtricitabine (FTC), and Efavirenz (EFV). This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. If the preferred regimen is contraindicated or unavailable, alternative regimens include combinations of Zidovudine (AZT), 3TC, and EFV or Nevirapine (NVP). The use of Stavudine (d4T) in first-line regimens should be discontinued due to its significant metabolic toxicities. 5. Infant Prophylaxis: Infants of mothers receiving ART and breastfeeding should receive six weeks of daily Nevirapine (NVP) prophylaxis. For infants on replacement feeding, four to six weeks of daily NVP or twice-daily AZT prophylaxis is recommended. 6. Second-Line ART Regimens: For adults and adolescents, second-line ART should consist of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). After failure of a TDF-based first-line regimen, AZT + 3TC is recommended as the NRTI backbone for second-line therapy. Conversely, after failure of an AZT or d4T-based first-line regimen, TDF + 3TC (or FTC) is recommended. Heat-stable fixed-dose combinations of Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) and Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) are the preferred boosted PI options. 7. Third-Line ART Regimens: National programs should develop policies for third-line ART, which should include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as integrase inhibitors and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs. Patients on failing second-line regimens with no new ARV options should continue with a tolerated regimen while exploring adherence strategies. 8. Operational and Service Delivery Recommendations: Decentralization of ART services is encouraged, with initiation in hospitals and maintenance at peripheral health facilities or community levels. Task-shifting is recommended, allowing trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses to initiate and maintain ART. Community health workers can dispense ART between clinical visits. Mobile phone text messages may be used as reminders to improve ART adherence. 9. Guidance for Program Managers: National authorities should adopt a transparent and inclusive decision-making process when implementing clinical and operational recommendations. This process should consider local HIV epidemiology, health system capacity, and resource availability. Monitoring and evaluation systems should be strengthened to track the implementation and impact of new recommendations. 10. Consolidated Guidelines: The WHO has combined previous guidelines on ART for adults, adolescents, children, and PMTCT into a single, harmonized document. The guidelines emphasize a public health approach, focusing on simplified and harmonized ART regimens, earlier diagnosis, and expanded access to treatment and prevention services. These recommendations aim to optimize HIV care and treatment, improve health outcomes, and reduce HIV transmission globally.
